claims.text: Most existing learning-to-defer methods make instance-level routing decisions, whereas segmentation requires spatially varying decisions near ambiguous boundaries, low-contrast tissues and small lesions.
DeferredSeg adds J+1 pixel-wise routing channels for a base segmentor and J experts while retaining the original segmentation output channels.

The Deferral Collaboration loss rewards correct expert predictions, suppresses incorrect expert routing, rewards the model branch when its thresholded prediction is correct, and supervises segmentation probabilities with binary cross-entropy.

Training combines collaboration loss, spatial-coherence loss and a load-balancing penalty; the latter penalizes batch-average soft expert routing probabilities outside configurable lower and upper bounds.

At inference, each pixel is assigned to the branch with the largest routing logit. Model-routed pixels use the base prediction thresholded at 0.5; expert-routed pixels use the selected expert's prediction.
The auxiliary CNN aggregated deferral predictor supports spatial-coherence training; at inference it is used only for visualization and does not determine hard routing or final fusion.

Evaluation uses synthetic expert masks on PROMISE12, LiTS and AMOS22, and pre-existing clinician annotations as offline expert branches on Chaksu, QUBIQ and CURVAS; metrics are DSC, Jaccard and Sensitivity.

Synthetic masks and clinician annotations are proxies for prospective expert corrections. They provide predictions for selected pixels and are not routing inputs or determinants of where deferral occurs.
Comparative synthetic experts have foreground/background/boundary accuracy profiles of 92/98/98%, 85/99/94% and 75/95/90%, respectively.
QUBIQ reference masks use STAPLE fusion of annotations disjoint from the expert branches; Chaksu and CURVAS consensus references derive from the same annotation pool used for expert branches.
PatchCorr uses the same expert source as one-expert DeferredSeg, with its correction budget matched to DeferredSeg's one-expert deferral ratio on each dataset.
On synthetic-expert PROMISE12, System DSC is 97.06±0.05% with one expert and 96.00±0.14% with three experts, compared with 86.17±1.53% for fine-tuned MedSAM and 92.24±0.03% for PatchCorr.
PROMISE12 deferral ratios are 4.32% with one synthetic expert and 10.28% with three; the corresponding model-retained proportions are 95.68% and 89.72%.
In offline QUBIQ brain-growth evaluation, System DSC increases from 83.15% for fine-tuned MedSAM to 86.68% with one expert and 89.33% with three experts.

On offline QUBIQ prostate evaluation, one- and three-expert System DSC values are 96.73% and 95.71%, versus 94.77% for fine-tuned MedSAM; Sensitivity decreases from 96.20% to 93.69% and 92.76%, respectively.

One-sided paired Wilcoxon tests find significant case-level DSC improvements over fine-tuned MedSAM in 15/16 comparisons for each expert configuration, over PatchCorr in 16/16 for each configuration, and over CENet-FT in all six CENet tasks.
The non-significant comparisons against fine-tuned MedSAM are AMOS22 liver with one expert and LiTS liver with three experts.
In the PROMISE12 three-expert ablation, DC alone yields 95.39±1.64% System DSC, DC+SC yields 95.79±1.71%, DC+LB yields 96.59±1.46%, and all three losses yield 96.58±1.04%.
Adding experts does not guarantee better performance: benefits depend on regional complementarity and the target task.
Training still requires previously annotated expert data, and the real-expert evaluation is offline; broader prospective studies are needed to assess clinical generality and interaction efficiency.

A proof-of-concept Streamlit interface demonstrates expert-region assignment, local correction and fusion, but usability, annotation time, interaction cost and clinical efficiency remain unevaluated in prospective clinician studies.
The contribution is a pixel-wise medical segmentation deferral framework with collaboration and spatial-coherence losses, multi-expert load balancing, and instantiations on MedSAM and CENet.
